title: Car accident on the Queensborough Bridge
summary: Heading to a composition class at NYU, Freeman was hit head-on by a truck, breaking nine ribs, and was treated at a Harlem hospital refusing narcotics.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yes, that's very nice, isn't it. Bud, I'll tell you one thing you didn't -- about this time, I didn't know that you were in a car smash, in '67 or '68.

Yes, as I said, I had been coming to Europe to the U.K. two and three times a year, and then I got into a -- you see the World's Greatest Jazz Band hadn't begun yet. We were doing -- we had done some things for Gibson, out in Colorado, in Denver and then I was living in New York, I was married, I enrolled at New York University, to take a class in composition. There was a fine Viennese composer by the name of Sussmann Shyman who was into some pretty deep stuff and I wanted to study with this guy just as a non-entity. I didn't --
Yes, to study composition, and my first class was to start that night at 8:25 and that afternoon I was in an automobile accident, riding --
Well, I was riding from Long Island, we were going over the Queensborough Bridge and the man with me

was a good driver and we weren't going very fast, but we were over on the left side and there was traffic coming toward us which was stalled, and a man in a little white truck pulled out for no reason at all and hit us headon, but luckily, we skidded into him, by the time he put the skids we might not have been going more than 20 miles an hour. But you can imagine, it's a headon thing -- I don't know -- I don't know that we had a belt, there weren't seat belts, but I know that I didn't use one and I saw it coming. I had maybe two or three seconds warning, and I just instinctively threw my right arm up over my eyes thinking there would be broken glass and all that, and I was thrown into this sharp dashboard and I had a multiple fracture of the right ribcage, broke nine ribs.

I wasn't knocked out. I got out of the car under my own strength and our car looked like an accordion, you should have seen it, it was incredible that we weren't killed, and just then a taxi was going by on the bridge and he took me, 96 th I lived up on 9th Street between Park and Madison, and he got me to my home in 20 minutes, and I had two of my ex-wife's aunts, two old Louisville belles were there, and I said get me a tall straight drink of vodka, which I drank down, got pretty drunk to lessen the pain and call a doctor.
So they got in touch with my wife who was teaching, she was a child therapist, she was teaching down in her office,

and she called her doctor, who came over and he gave me a shot and took me in the hospital wagon to the best, incidentally, best bone hospital, one of the best in the world, 124th and Madison, in Harlem.

I don't remember, I am not very good with names, but it was an excellent hospital. You see, they didn't bind me up, I was just left to heal by myself and I took no -- they said, I don't think you're going to be able to stand the pain, we may have to put you on something. I said, no, I don't want any narcotics, I'll take the pain and found out that I have sort of a high pain threshold, or at least I was able to go through that.
